C005.subject: GDP per capita growth rate
C005.object: subjective life satisfaction among the top income quintile in high-income countries
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: GDP per capita growth rate subjective life satisfaction among the top income quintile in high-income countries]

[PATH:empirical] Panel data from the World Values Survey (WVS) and European Social Survey (ESS) linked to OECD national accounts (1990-2020) for top income quintile respondents — Directly tests the correlation between GDP per capita growth and subjective life satisfaction within the top income quintile across multiple OECD countries over the specified period, controlling for individual-level confounds.

[PATH:literature] Re-analysis of the Easterlin Paradox literature focusing on relative income effects and hedonic adaptation among high-income groups — Provides theoretical and empirical context for why growth might not translate to increased satisfaction for the wealthy, due to social comparison and diminishing marginal utility of income gains.

[PATH:empirical] Experimental or quasi-experimental studies on income windfalls (e.g., lottery winners, stock market booms) and subsequent life satisfaction changes in high-income contexts — Offers causal evidence on whether unexpected income growth reduces satisfaction (e.g., via status anxiety or increased expectations) among already affluent individuals.

C006.subject: GDP per capita
C006.object: material living standards in high-income countries
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: GDP per capita material living standards in high-income countries]

[PATH:empirical] OECD Better Life Index data on subjective well-being, income distribution, and non-market goods (e.g., leisure, environmental quality) for high-income countries — Directly compares GDP per capita with multidimensional measures of material living standards, allowing assessment of divergence in high-income economies since the late 20th century.

[PATH:literature] Piketty, Saez, and Zucman (2018) 'Distributional National Accounts' for the United States and other high-income countries — Provides evidence on how GDP per capita growth has been distributed across income groups, revealing whether aggregate growth reflects typical material living standards or is skewed toward top earners.

[PATH:theoretical] Stiglitz-Sen-Fitoussi Commission (2009) and subsequent reports on 'Beyond GDP' indicators — Establishes the theoretical and methodological case for why GDP per capita may misrepresent material living standards, particularly in wealthy nations where non-monetary factors (e.g., health, social connections) are significant.

qualifier.geographic: high-income countries as defined by the World Bank

C007.subject: increased GDP growth
C007.object: population-level social cohesion indices over a 10-year lag
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: increased GDP growth population-level social cohesion indices over a 10-year lag]

[PATH:empirical] Longitudinal analysis of OECD Social Expenditure Database (SOCX) merged with Gallup World Poll social cohesion indices and national GDP growth rates, using fixed-effects models with 10-year lags. — Directly tests the hypothesized negative correlation between GDP growth and social cohesion over the specified lag, controlling for country-level confounds and temporal autocorrelation.

[PATH:literature] Review of the 'Easterlin Paradox' and related literature on economic growth and subjective well-being, particularly studies examining social trust, civic participation, and community engagement as mediators. — Provides theoretical grounding and empirical precedent for why rapid economic growth might erode social cohesion (e.g., through inequality, urbanization, or cultural disruption), and identifies gaps in existing evidence for the 10-year lag structure.

[PATH:empirical] Comparative case studies of OECD countries with high GDP growth but divergent social cohesion trajectories (e.g., South Korea vs. Ireland) using qualitative process tracing and interrupted time series analysis. — Helps isolate causal mechanisms and assess whether the correlation is robust across different institutional and cultural contexts, addressing potential omitted variable bias.

C008.subject: GDP
C008.object: essential economic foundations for non-material dimensions of wellbeing
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: GDP essential economic foundations for non-material dimensions of wellbeing]

[PATH:empirical] Cross-country panel data on GDP per capita and subjective well-being (e.g., World Happiness Report, Gallup World Poll) controlling for income inequality, social trust, and health outcomes — Tests whether GDP captures foundational economic conditions that enable non-material wellbeing (e.g., life satisfaction, meaning) after accounting for other factors.

[PATH:empirical] Longitudinal studies of economic shocks (e.g., recessions, rapid growth) and their impact on non-material dimensions like community cohesion, mental health, and perceived autonomy (e.g., data from national health surveys or time-use studies) — Examines causal links between GDP changes and non-material wellbeing, isolating GDP's role as a foundation versus a proxy.

[PATH:theoretical] Theoretical literature on 'capabilities approach' (Sen, Nussbaum) and 'beyond GDP' frameworks (e.g., Stiglitz-Sen-Fitoussi Commission reports) — Provides conceptual grounding to evaluate whether GDP captures essential economic foundations (e.g., resources for capabilities) or misses key non-material prerequisites.

C009.subject: GDP growth
C009.object: human wellbeing inequality more than it reduces poverty in contexts of environmental degradation
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: GDP growth human wellbeing inequality more than it reduces poverty in contexts of environmental degradation]

[PATH:empirical] Longitudinal panel data from the World Bank's Living Standards Measurement Study (LSMS) and the Global Environment Facility's environmental degradation indices for selected developing economies (e.g., Indonesia, Nigeria, Brazil) from 2000-2020 — Directly tests the hypothesis by linking GDP growth to changes in both poverty rates (e.g., $1.90/day headcount) and inequality metrics (e.g., Gini coefficient), while controlling for environmental degradation indicators (e.g., deforestation, air pollution, water stress).

[PATH:literature] Systematic review of studies on the 'resource curse' and 'green growth' in high-inequality, resource-extractive economies (e.g., papers in World Development, Ecological Economics) — Synthesizes existing evidence on how GDP growth in such contexts often exacerbates inequality through rent capture and displacement, while poverty reduction is offset by environmental health costs, providing a theoretical and empirical foundation for the claim.

[PATH:theoretical] Agent-based or computable general equilibrium (CGE) model calibrated to a representative developing economy with high inequality and resource extraction (e.g., based on Zambia or Ghana) — Simulates counterfactual scenarios where GDP growth occurs under varying levels of environmental degradation, allowing isolation of the differential impact on poverty versus inequality, and testing sensitivity to key parameters (e.g., resource rent distribution, pollution exposure).

scope.domain: developing economies with high inequality and high resource extraction

qualifier.geographic: developing economies with high inequality and high resource extraction

C010.subject: GDP growth
C010.object: human wellbeing regardless of inequality or environmental conditions
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: GDP growth human wellbeing regardless of inequality or environmental conditions]

[PATH:empirical] Longitudinal household survey data (e.g., Demographic and Health Surveys, LSMS) combined with subnational GDP estimates for developing economies (1980-2020) — Allows direct test of whether GDP growth correlates with changes in objective and subjective wellbeing indicators (e.g., health, education, life satisfaction) while controlling for inequality and environmental degradation at the local level.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of studies on the 'Easterlin Paradox' and the 'Threshold Hypothesis' in developing economies — Synthesizes existing evidence on whether the GDP-wellbeing link holds beyond a certain income threshold or when inequality and environmental costs are factored in, providing a broad empirical and theoretical check on the hypothesis.

[PATH:theoretical] Theoretical models incorporating inequality and environmental externalities into growth-utility frameworks (e.g., Dasgupta, 2021; Stiglitz-Sen-Fitoussi Commission) — Formally examines whether GDP growth can be a sufficient condition for wellbeing gains when inequality and environmental degradation are present, offering a logical refutation or confirmation of the hypothesis' core assumption.
